![](assets/art/theme-interdisciplinary.webp){.banner fig-alt="Overlapping colored circles representing different fields"}

Environmental problems cut across fields. I draw on the social sciences to understand people, policy, and power, and on the quantitative sciences to measure what's happening on the ground.

Transdisciplinary work goes one step further, bringing in the knowledge of communities, agencies, and practitioners outside academia so the research answers questions people in Florida are actually asking.

## A Short History of Interdisciplinary &amp; Transdisciplinary Research

Working across fields is an old idea, but it took off as researchers faced problems no single discipline could solve.

```{=html}
<details class="history">
<summary><span class="sum-open">Show the timeline</span><span class="sum-close">Hide the timeline</span> <span class="sum-meta">9 moments, 1959–2012</span></summary>
<ol class="timeline">
  <li class="era">Two cultures</li>
  <li><span class="yr">1959</span><div><h4><em>The Two Cultures</em></h4><p>C. P. Snow warns that the sciences and humanities have stopped talking to each other.</p></div></li>
  <li><span class="yr">1970</span><div><h4>Transdisciplinarity is named</h4><p>Jean Piaget uses the term at an OECD seminar on interdisciplinary teaching and research.</p></div></li>
  <li class="era">Problems that cross boundaries</li>
  <li><span class="yr">1973</span><div><h4>Wicked problems</h4><p>Horst Rittel and Melvin Webber argue planning problems have no single right answer and can't be solved by one discipline.</p></div></li>
  <li><span class="yr">1984</span><div><h4>Complexity science</h4><p>The Santa Fe Institute is founded to study complex systems across physics, biology, economics, and social science.</p></div></li>
  <li><span class="yr">1994</span><div><h4>Mode 2 knowledge</h4><p>Michael Gibbons and colleagues describe research that is organized around real-world problems instead of disciplines.</p></div></li>
  <li class="era">Science with society</li>
  <li><span class="yr">2001</span><div><h4>Sustainability science</h4><p>Robert Kates and colleagues call for a new field linking nature and society to support sustainable development.</p></div></li>
  <li><span class="yr">2004</span><div><h4><em>Facilitating Interdisciplinary Research</em></h4><p>The U.S. National Academies recommend ways for universities and funders to support work across fields.</p></div></li>
  <li><span class="yr">2009</span><div><h4>Social-ecological systems</h4><p>Elinor Ostrom publishes a framework for studying how people and ecosystems shape each other.</p></div></li>
  <li><span class="yr">2012</span><div><h4>Transdisciplinary practice</h4><p>Daniel Lang and colleagues set out principles for research that includes communities and practitioners from the start.</p></div></li>
</ol>
</details>
```

## Key Readings

- Gibbons, M., et al. (1994). <em>The New Production of Knowledge</em>. Sage.
- Kates, R. W., et al. (2001). Sustainability science. <em>Science</em>, 292(5517), 641–642.
- Lang, D. J., et al. (2012). Transdisciplinary research in sustainability science: Practice, principles, and challenges. <em>Sustainability Science</em>, 7(S1), 25–43.
- Ostrom, E. (2009). A general framework for analyzing sustainability of social-ecological systems. <em>Science</em>, 325(5939), 419–422.
- Rittel, H. W. J., &amp; Webber, M. M. (1973). Dilemmas in a general theory of planning. <em>Policy Sciences</em>, 4(2), 155–169.
